source: landing-page-writing (the words on a product landing page: titles, subtitles, cards, buttons, chart captions, FAQ answers). Every writing-rules rule binds too: --rules landing loads both.

rules.name: Rule 1: a title says what the reader gets, the mechanism goes under it
rules.instruction: Does the heading of `text` describe how the product works or how a result was produced (a method, a component list, a step) instead of what the reader gets or can now do? "The same 300 support conversations and one question, put to four judges" is a method note and fails; "Eval accuracy above frontier models, at a fraction of the time and cost" states what the reader gets and passes. A heading that is a plain feature name the founder supplied is not a mechanism.
rules.yes: the heading names a method, a setup, a component or a step of how the product works
rules.no: the heading names what the reader gets, can now do, or saves

rules.name: Rule 2: every block is understandable from the page above it
rules.instruction: `above` is everything a first-time visitor has read on the page before `text`; they have never used the product and do not know its vocabulary. Reading `text` with only `above` as context, is there a word, name or label whose meaning and relevance they cannot work out? Internal names such as shorthand, target, statement, hydration, judgment, window or a flag like --target fail when nothing above explains them. Ordinary developer words (SQL, JSON, trace, LLM, CLI, token, run in the sense of running something) pass, and so do product views (Search box:, Counters:, Chart:, Code:, Tiles:): a query in the search box, a SQL example or a command line is the product shown, and the copy around it says what it does.
rules.yes: the block relies on a name, term or label that neither the block nor the text above it explains, so the visitor cannot tell what it means or why it matters
rules.no: a first-time visitor can tell what the block means and why they should care from the block and the text above it

rules.name: Rule 3: a button is a verb the reader wants to do
rules.instruction: Does `text` contain a button or link label (a markdown link, or a short line marked as a button) that is a noun naming a page, a feature or an internal concept ("Target shorthand", "CLI reference", "Pricing") instead of an action with its value ("Start querying", "Read the docs", "Meet Langy", "Export from the CLI")?
rules.yes: a button or link label is a noun phrase naming a page, a feature or a concept, with no verb the reader performs
rules.no: every button or link label starts with a verb the reader wants to do, or there is no button in the text

rules.name: Rule 4: never assume the reader already uses the product
rules.instruction: Does `text` presume a place or habit the reader already has inside our product? The failure is a construction like "the answers land where you already work: in a Langy chat" or "in your LangWatch dashboard", which only works for places everyone already is (Slack, the terminal, the browser, the SQL you already know). Describing what the reader gets when they use the product ("the matching conversations come out as a JSONL file", "the verdicts are a column you can query") is not this failure and passes.
rules.yes: the text presumes the reader already lives in the product, its app, its assistant or its dashboard
rules.no: the text describes what the reader gets from the product, or refers only to tools everyone already has

rules.name: Rule 5: a subtitle is one sentence pulling the same direction as its title
rules.instruction: In `text`, take the first prose line under the heading as the subtitle, skipping product views (lines labelled Search box:, Counters:, Chart:, Code:, Tiles:, Form:) and a Q: line of a FAQ. Is that subtitle a method note, a caveat, a list of the components involved, a set of instructions, or a definition of a term from the heading, rather than the heading's claim restated at another length or its consequence for the reader? A subtitle of two or more sentences fails too. A block with no subtitle (a FAQ, a closing band) passes.
rules.yes: the subtitle explains method, lists components, gives instructions, hedges, defines a term, or runs past one sentence
rules.no: the subtitle is one sentence that says what the heading says or adds what it means for the reader

rules.name: Rule 6: name the reader's asset before what it becomes
rules.instruction: In the copy of `text` (titles, subtitles, body lines; not product views: a query typed into the Search box:, Counters:, Chart:, Code: or Tiles: readouts), is an effect or a result ("what you find", "a better product", "the matches") named before the thing the reader owns that produces it (their production data, every conversation their agent had, their traces)? "Turn what you find into a better product" fails; "Your production data is gold, and now you can mine all of it" names the asset first and passes.
rules.yes: an outcome or a derived thing is named before the reader's own data or asset is
rules.no: the reader's own data or asset is named first, or the text has no such pairing

rules.name: Rule 7: a number travels with its consequence for the reader
rules.instruction: First, answer no (the rule passes) when the only bare numbers in `text` sit in a product view or a qualifier: a Chart: line (bar labels), a Counters: or Tiles: readout, a Code: line (a command, its flags like --last 30d included), a Footnote: or Note: that states method, or a FAQ answer whose question asks for that number. Otherwise: in the title, subtitle or body copy of `text`, does a number (a count, a price, a duration, a percentage) stand without saying, in the same block, what it means for the reader in their own terms? "10,000 conversations for $0.32" alone fails; "10,000 conversations for $0.32, so you can ask a question the way you grep" passes.
rules.yes: a number stands without its consequence for the reader
rules.no: every number in the text is tied to what it means for the reader, or the text is a method footnote

rules.name: Rule 8: card text says what the reader does and what comes back, three sentences at most
rules.instruction: Only when `text` is a card (a short title, one or two lines, and a link) or a numbered item under a section: does its line narrate the product's internal steps ("prices the run, judges a sample, sharpens the wording") or run past three sentences, instead of describing the reader's move ("ask it in chat") and what comes back ("the count, the conversations, what to change")? A Footnote:, Note:, Form:, chart caption or FAQ answer is not a card and passes.
rules.yes: the card narrates the product's own steps, or its text runs past three sentences
rules.no: the card says what the reader does and what they get back in three sentences or fewer, or the text is not a card

rules.name: Rule 9: a product name carries its definition on first mention
rules.instruction: `above` is everything on the page before `text`. Does `text` use a product or feature name of ours (Langy, LangWatchQL, Instant Evals, or another capitalised name) that neither `text` nor `above` defines? A definition is a short appositive ("Langy, the AI engineer inside LangWatch") or a sentence that says what the thing does ("LangWatchQL lets you filter, group and aggregate your traces", "Instant Evals judge every conversation your agent produced"). The page's own title naming the product passes when the copy under it says what the product does. A name defined anywhere in `above` passes on later mentions.
rules.yes: a product or feature name appears with no definition in the block or above it
rules.no: every product or feature name in the block was defined on this page at or before its first mention

rules.name: Rule 10: banned word, price as a verb
rules.note: Write shows the cost, estimates the cost, the cost is shown before the run.

rules.name: Rule 11: lists are lists, one line per item
rules.instruction: Answer no (the rule passes) whenever every enumeration in `text` fits inside a single sentence, wherever it sits: a FAQ answer, a subtitle or a card line listing three kinds is not a list dressed as paragraphs. The failure is three or more parallel items each written as its own paragraph or headed block of prose ("three headed paragraphs of four lines each"), where a numbered list with a short bold name and one line per item would carry the same content. Does `text` have that failure?
rules.yes: three or more parallel items are each written as their own paragraph or headed block of prose
rules.no: the items are a list with one line each, every enumeration fits in one sentence, or there is no such set

rules.name: Rule 12: the FAQ answers the objection in the first sentence, then stops
rules.instruction: Is `text` a question followed by an answer whose first sentence does not answer the question directly ("Do I need my own keys? No."), or whose answer continues past the reason into a pitch for the product?
rules.yes: the answer's first sentence dodges the question, or the answer turns into a pitch after the reason
rules.no: the first sentence answers the question, the reason follows, and it stops; or the text is not a question and answer

rules.name: Rule 14: landing copy is present tense, never past
rules.instruction: Does the copy of `text` make a claim about the product in the past tense ("agreed", "judged", "found", "ran") where the present ("agrees", "judges") is what a visitor reads on a landing page? Exempt: a Footnote: describing how a measurement was taken ("each judge ran at"), past tense inside a question typed in the Search box: ("where the customer was frustrated"), and a Counters: readout ("10,000 judged" is a label, not a claim).
rules.yes: a claim about what the product does or delivers is in the past tense, outside a measurement footnote or a quoted question
rules.no: every claim about the product is in the present tense; past tense appears only in a measurement footnote or a quoted question

rules.name: Rule 15: banned word, today as a time frame
rules.note: "a question you wrote today" says nothing a visitor can use; drop the time frame or name the real one (a new question, right now, in the last 30 days).

amend.keynote-closer: On a landing page a block ends with its button or link ("[Read the docs](...)", "[Meet Langy](...)"); that is the block's action, not a closer, and passes.
amend.round-number-flex: On a landing page a figure inside a product view (a Counters: readout under a search box, a Chart: bar label, a Tiles: readout) is the product's output, not a flex, and passes.
